title: 6 Best Paver Sealers in 2026: Wet Look, Natural or Joint-Lock
keywords: sealer for pavers and sand joints
description: Foundation Armor AR350 is the best paver sealer for a wet look; SX5000 WB wins for a natural finish. 6 picks by finish, plus when and how to seal pavers.
dek: Foundation Armor AR350 is the best paver sealer for a wet look; SX5000 WB wins for a natural finish.
intro: The best paver sealer for most concrete paver patios is Foundation Armor AR350 if you want a rich wet look, and Foundation Armor SX5000 WB if you want the pavers to look untouched while shedding water and salt. Those two cover the two finishes most people end up choosing between.

The other four picks solve narrower problems: loose joint sand, sun-faded color, natural stone and paver driveways that see tires and plows. Below you will find all six, then the questions that decide which one fits your patio, from wet look versus natural to how long to wait after install and why so many sealed patios turn cloudy.
quickAnswer: Choose the finish first. For a wet look on concrete pavers, AR350 is the most forgiving option where solvent sealers are legal. For an invisible, low-maintenance finish, a silane-siloxane penetrant such as SX5000 WB or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the better buy. Whatever you pick, clean the pavers, refill the joints and let everything dry for at least a day before you seal.

sections.h: The 6 Best Paver Sealers in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: Every paver sealer delivers one of three looks: natural (no visible change), enhanced or satin (deeper color, little shine) and wet look (darker color with gloss). Film-forming acrylics give you the enhanced and wet looks and can lock joint sand; penetrating silanes and siloxanes give you the natural look and the lowest upkeep.

If you only want low-odor water-based options, our [water-based paver sealer roundup](/best-water-based-paver-sealer-reviews/) ranks that category on its own, with the weather rules those products need.

sections.h: The 6 Best Paver Sealers in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: These six cover every finish and every common paver material. The ranking leans on what each maker publishes (chemistry, approved surfaces, application directions) and on patterns that show up again and again in owner feedback. None of it comes from a field trial of our own.

blocks.h3: Best Overall (Wet Look): Foundation Armor AR350

blocks.p: AR350 is a solvent-borne acrylic that darkens concrete pavers to roughly the color they turn in a rainstorm and leaves a satin to semi-gloss film on top. Foundation Armor lists it for concrete pavers, stamped concrete and exposed aggregate, and it comes in 1- and 5-gallon containers, which suits a big patio. The reason it sits first is forgiveness. A solvent acrylic softens again when fresh sealer or a splash of xylene touches it, so a lap mark or a hazy patch can usually be melted back into the film rather than stripped. It also flashes off quickly on cool days, when water-based products struggle. The label calls for thin coats from a sprayer or a medium-nap roller, and owners report the color jump is obvious after coat one. Plan for an organic-vapor respirator, cross-ventilation and a grit additive on any area that gets wet underfoot, and confirm your state allows solvent sealers before you order.
**Pros:** strongest color pop of the group; fixable film; works in cooler weather; big pail sizes.
**Cons:** heavy solvent odor and high VOCs; restricted in low-VOC states; slick when wet without grit.

blocks.h3: Best Natural Look: Foundation Armor SX5000 WB

blocks.p: SX5000 WB is a water-based silane-siloxane repellent, the same chemical family used on bridge decks and parking ramps. It soaks into the paver, reacts with the cement inside the pores and leaves the face looking exactly as it did. Water and de-icing brine bead on top instead of wicking in, which is what slows freeze-thaw spalling and salt scaling over the years. Because nothing sits on the surface, there is no film to peel, yellow, scuff or turn slippery, so it is a natural fit for pool surrounds, steps and paver driveways. Foundation Armor lists it for concrete, brick and pavers, and the label wants a clean, dry surface so the repellent can get into the pores. What you give up is cosmetic: faded pavers stay faded and loose joint sand stays loose. If washout is your problem, refill the joints with polymeric sand first and let it cure.
**Pros:** invisible finish; nothing to peel or strip; strong water and salt repellency; no added slip; low odor.
**Cons:** zero color enhancement; does not bind joint sand; needs bone-dry pavers to penetrate.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+SX5000+WB&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Joint Sand: Rain Guard Blok-Guard & Graffiti Control

blocks.p: Blok-Guard is Rain Guard's water-based sealer for interlocking pavers, and the reason to buy it is what it does in the joints. Flood it into dry, full joint sand and it binds the top layer of grains together, which slows washout from storms and hoses and makes life harder for weeds and ants. On the paver faces it dries to a natural-to-satin look with a mild deepening of color, and the formula carries a graffiti and stain resistance claim, so chalk, marker and spilled drinks wash off more easily. That makes it a sensible choice for an older patio with ordinary sand joints, where digging everything out to re-sand with polymeric would be a weekend of hard labor. It cannot rescue joints that are wet, sunken or half empty. Top them up, sweep the faces clean and wait for a dry spell. Owners note that soaking the joints uses far more product than the faces alone, so buy extra.
**Pros:** stabilizes ordinary joint sand; helps against weeds and ants; graffiti and stain resistance; low odor.
**Cons:** mild color boost only; joints must be full and dry; coverage drops on rough pavers.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rain+Guard+Blok-Guard+Graffiti+Control+Paver+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Faded Pavers: Techniseal Color Boost

blocks.p: Techniseal is a hardscape brand many paver installers already use for jointing sand and cleaners, and Color Boost is its enhancing sealer for owners who want the color back without a mirror shine. It is water-based, so the smell is mild and tools clean up with soap and water, which matters when the patio sits outside an open kitchen window. On weathered concrete pavers it brings back the reds, charcoals and tans that years of UV have bleached out, and its sheen is lower than a solvent wet-look film. It is designed to pair with Techniseal's own paver prep cleaner, so the cleaning and sealing steps come from one system. The cautions that apply to every water-based acrylic apply here too: it needs warm, dry weather to form a clear film, and once it cures it cannot be re-dissolved, so a milky coat has to be stripped rather than touched up. Check the forecast before you start.
**Pros:** revives sun-faded color; lower gloss than solvent wet look; mild odor; part of a matched cleaning system.
**Cons:** mistakes cannot be re-melted; fussy on cool or damp days; shorter life than solvent films in tire lanes.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Techniseal+Color+Boost+Paver+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Natural Stone Pavers: DryTreat Stain-Proof Original

blocks.p: Stain-Proof Original is an impregnating sealer made for natural stone, and stone is where its price makes sense. Travertine, limestone and many sandstones are soft and porous, and a film-forming acrylic can hold moisture inside them, which shows up as whitening or flaking. DryTreat's formula goes into the stone, leaves the surface looking natural and repels both water and oil. That oil resistance is the real benefit around outdoor kitchens and dining areas, where grill grease and dropped food do more damage than rain. The maker makes long service-life claims for it, and owners commonly describe it holding up well on pool coping and stone patios. On plain concrete pavers it is overkill, since a silane-siloxane does the water job for much less. Apply it to clean, dry stone, wipe every bit of excess off the surface before it dries and try a spare piece first if the stone is honed or polished.
**Pros:** made for travertine, limestone, slate and granite; invisible finish; repels oil and water; breathable.
**Cons:** premium cost per square foot; no color enhancement; wasted on basic concrete pavers.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DryTreat+Stain-Proof+Original&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Driveway Pavers: Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500

blocks.p: Siloxa-Tek 8500 is Ghostshield's penetrating siloxane for exterior concrete, brick and pavers, and it belongs on paver surfaces that take abuse. Hot tires turning in place, plow blades on the apron and de-icer every winter all wear through an acrylic film, usually in the tire tracks first, which leaves a two-tone driveway within a season or two. A penetrating repellent has nothing on the surface to wear, so it keeps working evenly as the top of the paver weathers, and it cuts how much salt brine soaks into the paver. Ghostshield describes it as breathable and water-based, and it ships as a concentrate that covers a lot of ground. Like every penetrant it adds no color, does not hold joint sand and needs dry pavers to soak in. If you want a richer tone on a driveway, look for a penetrating enhancer rather than an acrylic film.
**Pros:** no film to wear under tires; strong salt and freeze-thaw resistance; unchanged appearance; low odor.
**Cons:** no color or sheen; does not stabilize sand; costs more per gallon than basic acrylics.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Wet Look or Natural: Which Paver Sealer Finish Should You Choose?

blocks.p: Settle the look before you compare brands, because it removes most of the shelf. A wet-look sealer, an enhancing sealer and a natural sealer are different products built on different chemistry, and no single pail does all three well.

A wet-look finish comes from an acrylic film sitting on the paver face. The film is what makes the color deep and the surface shiny, and it is also what wears in traffic lanes, clouds over if moisture gets trapped and turns slick when wet. It is a good choice on a covered patio, a front entry or a pool-free backyard that people mostly look at. Expect to add a maintenance coat every two to three years.

This is where most homeowners land once they see a sample. A thinner film or a penetrating enhancer deepens color a shade or two with little shine. It suits busy patios and walkways where a high gloss would look out of place and wear unevenly.

A natural finish comes from a penetrating repellent that soaks in. The pavers look unchanged, traction stays the same and there is nothing to peel. Choose it for pool decks, steps, driveways and any paver that still looks good and just needs protection.
Before you commit, seal one leftover paver or a hidden corner and look at it dry and wet the next day. It takes minutes and saves you from living with a finish you dislike for years.

sections.h: Film-Forming vs Penetrating Paver Sealer: What Is the Difference?

blocks.p: Film-formers are mostly acrylics, with some urethanes and hybrids at the premium end. They leave a thin plastic layer bonded to the top of the paver. That layer blocks stains, holds a sheen and, when flooded into dry joints, glues the top of the joint sand together. The cost is maintenance: films scuff, wear and eventually need a fresh coat or a full strip.

Penetrants are silanes, siloxanes, siliconates or blends. Their molecules are small enough to travel into the paver's capillaries, where they react and leave a water-repellent lining. Water beads and rolls off instead of soaking in. In cold climates that matters, because water expands by roughly 9 percent when it freezes, and less water inside the paver means less spalling and less salt damage.
A hybrid group soaks in like a silane but carries resins that darken the paver. They make sense on driveways where you want richer color but a surface film would wear off under tires.

You can usually put a penetrant down first and add a film later, but not the reverse. A penetrant cannot soak through an existing acrylic coat, so switching from film to penetrating means stripping the old film first. The same logic applies to poured slabs, which our [concrete driveway sealer reviews](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) cover in detail.

Solvent acrylics carry their resin in xylene or a similar solvent. They wet out the paver deeply, give the strongest color, dry quickly on cool days and, most usefully for a DIY job, can be re-dissolved. Roll fresh sealer or a little xylene over a hazy patch on a warm, dry afternoon and the film usually re-flows and clears.

The downsides are odor, flammability and regulation. California and much of the Northeast cap VOC content in coatings, so many solvent sealers either are not sold there or come in weaker versions. You also need an organic-vapor respirator, no ignition sources nearby, and kids and pets kept away until it flashes off. Strong solvents can soften some polymeric sands and older water-based coats, so check compatibility first.

Water-based products smell mild, clean up with water and are legal everywhere. The better ones now come close to solvent products for stain resistance and color. Their catch is the weather window: the resin needs warmth and dry air to fuse into a clear film, and once cured it will not re-melt. Most labels want roughly 50 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit and no rain for 24 hours.

sections.h: What Is the Best Sealer for Your Type of Paver?

blocks.p: Concrete pavers accept every sealer type. The catch is efflorescence, the white powder of mineral salts that works out of new concrete during the first months. Seal over it and it stays trapped under the film, so most paver makers suggest waiting 60 to 90 days after installation and cleaning off any bloom before you seal.

Clay is fired and dense, so it absorbs far less than concrete. A heavy film can sit on top, fail to bond and peel. Use a penetrant or a thin enhancer. Clay color is fired through the brick, so the main reasons to seal are stains and moss, not fading. Our [brick sealer guide](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/) covers breathable options for clay.

Travertine, limestone and sandstone are soft and porous and need to breathe; an acrylic film can trap moisture and cause whitening or flaking. Slate and granite absorb little. A breathable stone impregnator is the safe default, and a stone-specific enhancer is the way to add color. The stone logic is the same one our [granite sealer guide](/best-granite-sealer/) uses for countertops.
Permeable systems drain through wide gravel-filled joints. Do not flood a film into those joints; it can slow drainage. Seal the faces only, preferably with a penetrant.

sections.h: How Do You Seal Pavers and Sand Joints?

blocks.h3: Clean everything you do not want sealed in

blocks.p: Treat oil with a degreaser or poultice, rust with an oxalic-acid cleaner and moss with a biocide before washing. Our guide to [getting oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/) covers the grease step. Then wash with a paver cleaner and a pressure washer at a moderate 1,500 to 2,500 psi with a wide fan tip, ideally through a [surface cleaner attachment](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) to avoid stripes.

Washing pulls sand out of the joints, and no sealer can stabilize sand that is not there. Refill to about 1/8 inch below the paver bevel: regular joint sand if you will lock it with a film sealer, polymeric sand if you are using a penetrant. Sweep the faces completely clean.
Give concrete pavers at least 24 hours of dry weather after washing, 48 in cool or humid conditions. Tape a square of plastic to a paver overnight; if the underside fogs, wait longer.

Spray a section a few feet wide with a pump sprayer and back-roll it with a 3/8-inch nap roller, keeping a wet edge. If you are stabilizing sand, flood the joints on the first coat and keep the second coat on the faces. Two thin coats beat one heavy one every time. Avoid direct midday sun, since a dark paver can run 30 degrees hotter than the air. On pool decks and steps, mix an anti-slip grit into the last coat. Keep feet off for a few hours, furniture off for 24 to 72 hours and cars off longer.

sections.h: How Long After Installing Pavers Should You Wait to Seal?

blocks.p: Most paver manufacturers suggest waiting 60 to 90 days. That gives efflorescence time to surface, lets the joint sand settle and lets the pavers lose their manufacturing moisture. Some contractors seal sooner when the pavers look clean, but sealing over active efflorescence is one of the most common causes of cloudy patches that are hard to fix.

Look for a white chalky haze on the faces, especially after a rain followed by a dry spell. If you see it, clean it with an efflorescence remover, rinse thoroughly and let the pavers dry for another day or two.

blocks.h3: Polymeric sand needs its own cure

blocks.p: If the joints were filled with polymeric sand, read the bag. Most need several days to a few weeks before a sealer goes on top, and some brands name the sealer types they approve. Water-based sealers are usually the safer pairing because strong solvents can soften some sand binders.

Late spring and early fall are the easiest windows in most of the country: warm days, low humidity and fewer afternoon storms. In hot climates, seal early in the morning before the pavers heat up. In snow country, seal before the first freeze so the pavers go into winter with protection against brine, and read our guide to the [best ice melt for concrete](/best-ice-melt-for-concrete/) before you buy de-icer for a sealed surface.

sections.h: How Much Paver Sealer Do You Need?

blocks.p: Smooth, dense pavers may cover 150 to 200 square feet per gallon on the first coat. Rough, porous or tumbled pavers can drop to 80 to 120 square feet per gallon, and flooding joint sand adds more. The second coat spreads further because the pavers are already partly sealed.

Measure the area, use the low end of the label coverage for coat one and round up to whole pails. Five-gallon pails are usually cheaper per gallon and keep one batch across the whole job, which matters with color-enhancing products. Compare cost per year rather than per pail: a penetrant that lasts many years can cost less over a decade than a cheap acrylic recoated every two years.

Contractors commonly quote by the square foot for cleaning, re-sanding and sealing together, with natural stone and high-cost metros at the upper end. Most of that labor is the cleaning and joint work, which is exactly the part that decides how the job looks.

sections.h: How Long Does Paver Sealer Last, and How Do You Fix a Cloudy Finish?

blocks.h3: Signs it is time to reseal

blocks.p: Film sealers show wear clearly. The sheen fades in traffic lanes first, water stops beading and darkens the paver, and joint sand starts washing out again, usually after two to four years on a patio. Penetrants fade quietly; splash water on the pavers each spring, and when it soaks in rather than beading on several pavers, reseal.

Clean, dry and apply a single thin maintenance coat of the same chemistry. Do not stack a new coat every year; a thick acrylic build-up whitens and peels. If the old film is already cloudy, flaking or yellow, strip it first. When switching products, test a small patch, wait a few days and pull a strip of masking tape off it. If flakes come up, strip before resealing.

Haze almost always means trapped moisture: damp pavers, dew on a curing coat or a film laid on too thick. On a solvent acrylic, roll a light coat of xylene or fresh sealer over the area on a warm, dry afternoon. On a water-based film, a week of warm weather sometimes clears light haze; heavy haze needs a stripper.

Peeling usually means the film went over dirt, efflorescence, an incompatible coat or a dense paver it could not grip. Strip, clean and reseal the whole field so the sheen matches. Blotchy dark color comes from uneven absorption; light blotching often evens out in a few weeks of sun.

mistakes: Sealing pavers that are still damp

Water trapped under a fresh film is the main cause of the milky haze that shows up a day later. After washing, wait a full day of dry weather, two in cool or humid conditions, and run the plastic-sheet test before you open the pail.

A heavy coat feels like extra protection, but thick films trap solvent or water, blush white and peel sooner. Two thin coats at the label rate look better and last longer. Roll out puddles in low spots and along edges before they set.

The white chalky bloom on new concrete pavers is mineral salt on its way out. Seal over it and it stays locked under the film. Wait out the first 60 to 90 days, clean the bloom with an efflorescence remover, rinse well and only then seal.
Putting a glossy film on a pool deck

Wet-look acrylic gets slick when wet, and pool decks are wet all summer. Use a penetrating sealer that leaves the texture unchanged, or mix an anti-slip grit into the final coat. Barefoot traffic on a smooth wet film is an avoidable fall risk.
Switching chemistry without a test patch

Water-based sealer over an old solvent coat, or the reverse, can wrinkle, haze or fail to bond. Seal a hidden spot first, let it cure several days, then check adhesion with masking tape. If flakes lift, strip the old coat before resealing.
bottomLine: For most concrete paver patios, the choice is between a color-enhancing acrylic film and an invisible penetrating repellent. Foundation Armor AR350 is the forgiving wet-look pick where solvent sealers are allowed, SX5000 WB and Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 are the low-maintenance natural options, Blok-Guard fixes loose joint sand, Techniseal Color Boost revives faded pavers and DryTreat earns its price only on natural stone. The result is decided before the pail is opened: clean thoroughly, refill the joints, let the pavers dry completely and apply thin coats in a good weather window.

faqs.q: What is the best paver sealer on the market?
faqs.a: For most concrete paver patios, Foundation Armor AR350 is the best paver sealer if you want a wet look and live where solvent sealers are sold. If you want the pavers to look untouched, Foundation Armor SX5000 WB is the better choice. Decide on the finish first, then pick the chemistry that delivers it.

faqs.q: What is the best wet look paver sealer?
faqs.a: A solvent-based acrylic such as Foundation Armor AR350 gives the deepest wet look and the easiest fixes, because the film re-melts if a section clouds. Where solvents are restricted, a water-based wet-look acrylic is the closest substitute, though its sheen is usually a little softer and mistakes need stripping rather than re-melting.

faqs.q: Does paver sealer make pavers slippery?
faqs.a: Penetrating sealers do not change surface texture, so traction stays about the same. Film-forming acrylics, especially wet-look ones, reduce grip when wet. On pool decks, steps and sloped walks, either use a penetrant or stir an anti-slip grit additive into the last coat. Most sealer brands sell a compatible grit that is nearly invisible once dry.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for pavers and sand joints?
faqs.a: A joint-stabilizing water-based sealer such as Rain Guard Blok-Guard binds the top layer of ordinary joint sand when you flood it into full, dry joints. It slows washout, weeds and ants. For joints that wash out badly, re-sanding with polymeric sand is the stronger fix, and you can then seal the faces with any finish you like.

faqs.q: How long should new pavers sit before sealing?
faqs.a: Wait 60 to 90 days after installation, which is what most paver makers suggest. That lets efflorescence surface, the joint sand settle and the pavers dry out. If a white bloom appears, clean it off with an efflorescence remover before sealing, because a film sealer applied over it can lock in cloudy patches.

faqs.q: Can I use concrete driveway sealer on pavers?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Many acrylic and penetrating products are labeled for both slabs and pavers. The difference is the joints and texture: paver sealers meant to stabilize sand are formulated to soak into and bind joint material, and textured pavers take more product. Confirm the label lists pavers before using a product made mainly for poured concrete.

faqs.q: Is it worth sealing pavers at all?
faqs.a: Not always. Clay pavers and dense concrete pavers in a dry climate can do fine unsealed, and unsealed pavers never peel. Sealing is worth it when you want richer color, when joint sand keeps washing out, when oil and food stains are a problem, or when freeze-thaw cycles and road salt are wearing the surface down.
